target_customer: Developers (free users) and employers and recruiters who wanted to find or vet developers
problem: Developers had skills scattered across GitHub, Twitter and other sites with no single profile that employers trusted, and employers had no easy way to judge developer ability.
business_model: Developer profile network monetized through recruiting and job postings

founders.name: Matthew Deiters
founders.background_notes: TechCrunch (Feb 2012) names Matt Deiters as the founder. YC page bio lists later roles at Instacart, Cruise and Square, which came after Coderwall. No education or earlier employer found.

founders.name: Dave Newman
founders.background_notes: Listed as a founder on the YC page, current role cofounder and CTO of howie.com. No education or prior employer found.

competitors.name: GitHub profiles
competitors.what: Public code profiles where developers already showed work
competitors.traction_then: Named by TechCrunch as a place developers already display skills; Coderwall aggregated it

competitors.name: Stack Overflow
competitors.what: Q and A site whose reputation score signaled expertise
competitors.traction_then: Named by TechCrunch as an existing skill showcase and planned integration

technical_complexity.rationale: Pulled public data from GitHub, Twitter and LinkedIn APIs and computed badges and team rankings; standard web engineering for a two person team.

defensibility.rationale: Profiles and endorsements could build a small network, but the data came from other platforms and the badge concept was easy to copy.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No incumbent is documented copying it. The company ended up under Assembly, which by 2014 held the code and site.

market_need_then: In Feb 2012 TechCrunch reported about 13,000 profiles, roughly 20 percent monthly growth, sign ups driven entirely by Twitter, and some job postings asking applicants for a Coderwall profile.

branding.domain_note: Operates on coderwall.com, the exact .com, as of the 2012 coverage.

identity.mascot_or_character: Achievement badges with playful names such as Honey Badger and Altruist
identity.voice_and_tone: Playful developer culture tone via badge names

branding.brand_signature: Achievement badges such as Honey Badger 3 and Altruist
branding.community_and_virality: Sign ups came entirely from Twitter in early 2012 per TechCrunch; developers shared badges on profiles. No merch or fan accounts found.

brand_strength.rationale: Badges were a memorable hook and drove Twitter sharing, and the site still runs under the Coderwall name per a 2026 fetch, but no independent brand coverage was found.

outcome_analysis: Coderwall grew fast on Twitter driven sharing of its achievement badges and reached about 13,000 profiles within weeks of its YC debut in early 2012. YC lists it as acquired and its code later carried Assembly Made copyright notices, but no source gave the deal date, price or reason, and no funding rounds were found. The site still appeared live in a 2026 fetch, so it did not fail outright; why it stayed small is not public.
notes: Acquirer inferred from Crunchbase listing Assembly and 2014 Assembly Made copyright in repositories; no announcement found. Aggregator BounceWatch lists an undisclosed seed round dated 2012-03 with no investors; unverified so not recorded as a round. Company website coderwall.com fetched and appears live with a developer tips community and jobs board. Masterbranch was a possible competitor but no source dated near the batch was found, so it is left out. Completeness pass: the undisclosed seed dated 2012-03 (BounceWatch, led by Y Combinator) is now recorded and rests on that single database. VentureBeat reports Assembly, the successor founded by Dave Newman, Matthew Deiters and Chris Lloyd, raised 2.9M; that is a different entity and is not recorded as a Coderwall round, and the gap in Coderwall's own history is unknown.
